title: The jewels on loan (Midrash Mishlei 31)
hook: Beruriah breaks the news of their sons' deaths by asking about returning borrowed jewels

segments.voice: Yesterday Beruriah read the Psalm as sins, not sinners. Your line was end the sin, not the sinner. Today, a harder story from her life, told gently.

Today's story is about grief, so i'll go slowly. Maybe you've had to give someone terrible news, or someone had to give it to you. Either way, there's no good way to do it. The words are always too small, or too sudden. There's an old Jewish story about the hardest news there is, and about a mother who found a way to say it. It isn't in the Talmud. It comes from a later collection of teachings on the Book of Proverbs.
screen: `TODAY, SLOWLY.` → `THE HARDEST NEWS.` → `A MOTHER FINDS A WAY.`

segments.voice: The midrash on Proverbs tells it this way. One Shabbat afternoon, Rabbi Meir was teaching in the study house. While he was away, both of their sons died. Beruriah laid them on a bed in the upper room and covered them with a sheet. She said nothing during Shabbat. When Rabbi Meir came home after dark and the Sabbath had ended, she asked him a question. Some time ago, a man left something precious with me for safekeeping. Now he's come to take it back. Should I return it? Of course, said Rabbi Meir. Whoever holds something on deposit must give it back to its owner. Then she took him by the hand, led him upstairs, and pulled back the sheet. He wept. And she said: didn't you tell me we have to give back what was left with us? The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. Those words are from the Book of Job, and Jews still say them in grief today. The story doesn't pretend the loss is small. Rabbi Meir weeps. But it offers a way to hold it: what is loved was never owned. It was entrusted, for a while, and cared for. That isn't meant as an answer that makes grief stop. It's something to hold onto while grief does its work. And look at Beruriah: she carried the news alone through a whole day, so her husband could have his Shabbat.
screen: `TWO SONS, ONE SHABBAT.` · `SHOULD I RETURN WHAT WAS LENT?` · `THE LORD GAVE, THE LORD HAS TAKEN.` · `ENTRUSTED, NOT OWNED.` · then, large: `THEY WERE ON LOAN.`

segments.voice: If there's a loss in your life, a person, a place, a time, let it come to mind only as far as feels safe; you don't have to open it all the way, just sit next to it. Notice what you were given while you had it: one memory, one thing they taught you. If this is too much today, simply breathe, and think of someone you love who is here.
Beruriah, who told her husband of their sons' deaths by asking whether borrowed treasure should be returned.
Your line: they were on loan. What is loved is entrusted, not owned, and cared for a while. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: When Jews hear of a death they say the blessing baruch dayan ha-emet, blessed is the true Judge, and the line from Job, the Lord gave and the Lord has taken away, is often said at funerals.

fork.setup: you're Beruriah. your husband comes home after Shabbat, not knowing. how do you tell him?
options: tell him plainly, at the door.
ask him about returning something precious that was lent.
fork.reveal: she asked whether a deposit must be returned. he said yes. then she showed him, and quoted: the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away.

what a scholar hears: the midrash tells it on Proverbs 31:10, a woman of valor, praising Beruriah; it's much later than the Talmud.

notes: Midrash Mishlei on Proverbs 31:10 paraphrased; versions differ in details (e.g. whether the sons died on Shabbat afternoon while Meir was in the study house). The midrash is usually dated long after the Talmud.
Job 1:21 is paraphrased in modern English ('the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away') rather than quoted from JPS 1917.
Sensitive topic: the practice offers a way out ('if this is too much today'). A Keeper may want to review tone.
Some scholars note the story is a late addition to Beruriah's legend; the script says only that it's from a later collection.
